newsitem.title: POLAND: FOCUS-POLISH C.BANK EYES RATE RISE IN EARLY 1997.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-POLISH C.BANK EYES RATE RISE IN EARLY 1997.

text.p: The National Bank of Poland will wait for preliminary December inflation data before it decides if it has to raise official rates but fast credit growth is likely to make the decision unavoidable, its president said.

"We won't cause any surprises before the holidays, we will wait for some working figures on inflation in December...which is not a typical month because of vast demand for cash...but everything indicates that such a decision will be unavoidable," Hanna Gronkiewicz-Waltz told a news conference on Monday.

She said the rate rise might be forced by ballooning credit for households, which she said was likely to grow 100 percent this year. Corporate credit already grew 31 percent in the first 11 months of the year.
"It is the same situation as with the currency reserves boom in 1995 -- it is not the growth itself but its pace which is worrying us," the central bank chief said.
"The role of the NBP is an unpleasant one ... it is similar to the role of a person who comes to a swinging party and takes away the punch bowl," Gronkiewicz-Waltz said.

She said a rise of market rates to levels close to the bank's official lombard and discount rates, now at 25 percent and 22 percent respectively, would be a sign that the central bank's rates should be higher.
"It would be a very clear signal that our rates have to be increased...if market rates come close to ours," she said.

Gronkiewicz-Waltz added that credit expansion should stay at about 1.5 times the growth rate of the economy in order not to prompt a rate rise. Poland's economy is expected to grow between 5.5-6.5 percent this year against a seven percent rise in 1995.
"Now the real growth of credit for companies is already twice as big as the growth rate," she said.
Year-on-year inflation in November was 19.1 percent, down from 21.6 percent in December 1995, and is seen at around 18.5 percent at the end of this year.
Gronkiewicz-Waltz said the credit boom was likely to translate into faster price growth in six months.
"The current impulse will have an effect on inflation only in six months," she said.

The finance ministry has repeatedly criticised the idea of an interest rate increase by the independent central bank, saying there were other, more direct measures to curb credit growth, such as administrative lending limits.

But Gronkiewicz-Waltz dismissed the criticism saying the past showed banks knew how to by-pass administrative limits on credit and that such a move would also be a step backwards for the money market.
"It is a natural conflict of interests (between the finance ministry and the central bank) because higher interest rates mean higher costs of financing the public debt," she said.
